messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Hopelessness: I have no future, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For as long as he could remember, Marco had been the one people counted on to stay calm under pressure. Working as a prison guard at a medium-security facility outside Phoenix, he had learned to read a room before it turned, to keep his voice low and steady when others started shouting. He had never thought of himself as a happy person exactly, but he had been steady—that was the word his wife used. Steady. Then came the night shift in early March when his younger brother, Javier, was shot during a convenience store robbery two miles from Marco’s own house. Marco got the call from his mother at 3:17 a.m., still in uniform, sitting in the break room with a half-empty cup of coffee. By the time he reached the hospital, Javier was gone.

What Marco could not shake, what had lodged itself in his chest like a shard of glass, was the thought that he should have known. He worked in a world of violence. He saw the worst of people every day. He should have sensed something, said something, done something—called Javier that night, told him to stay home, driven over himself. The logic did not hold up to scrutiny, but logic had nothing to do with it. In the weeks after the funeral, Marco became certain that he had failed, that the universe had handed him a test and he had let everyone down. He stopped being able to look at his mother without feeling that he had betrayed her. When his wife tried to comfort him, he heard her words as accusations he deserved.

The first thing to change was his face. Marco noticed himself covering his mouth with his hand whenever someone spoke to him, pressing his palm against his lips as though trying to hold something back. Other times he would drag both hands down over his eyes and cheeks, a gesture that looked like exhaustion but felt, to him, like hiding. He did it without thinking, especially around the other guards. He did not want them to see what was underneath. He did not want to see it himself.

At work, Marco found himself picking fights. A coworker made an offhand comment about a prisoner’s family, and Marco was on his feet, voice rising, demanding to know what the man thought he knew about loss. The argument lasted twenty minutes, and afterward Marco felt a strange, hollow relief—the rush of anger had burned away the fog for a little while. He started doing it deliberately. He would needle a colleague about a minor mistake, or escalate a disagreement over shift scheduling into something personal. The drama was a kind of anesthesia. It gave him something to fight against that was not the image of Javier on a stretcher.

But the quieter moments were worse. When the unit fell silent, when he walked through the recreation yard and heard nothing but footsteps on concrete, the feeling crept back in—a sense that he was no longer quite inside his own body, that he was watching himself from a distance. He would go through the motions of his job, patting down an inmate, checking a lock, and part of him would be floating somewhere above, wondering if any of this was real. It frightened him more than any inmate ever had.

Marco began avoiding anything that touched the grief he was carrying. He stopped driving past the convenience store. He deleted the news app from his phone because every headline about a shooting or a family left behind felt like a message directed at him. When his wife mentioned a friend whose father had died, Marco stood up and walked out of the room. He could not bear to hear about other people losing someone. It was not sympathy he felt; it was a kind of raw, unbearable recognition.

He had come to believe that the person he used to be was gone. He told his wife one night, staring at the ceiling, that he used to be happy—or at least not miserable—and that version of himself had died with Javier. He saw no future. When she asked what he wanted, what he hoped for, he had no answer. The word “future” felt like a cruel joke.

What finally brought Marco to a therapist’s office was not insight or readiness. It was his wife, crying in the kitchen after he had snapped at her for asking how his day was. He saw her face, and he saw that he was doing to her what the trauma had done to him—isolating her, pushing her away, filling their home with tension he could not control. He agreed to come because he was tired of hiding behind his hands, tired of starting arguments he did not mean, tired of feeling like a ghost in his own life. He was afraid that if he did not change, he would lose the one person still standing beside him. And beneath that fear, buried so deep he could hardly name it, was a fragile hope that maybe, if he could face what had happened, he might one day stop feeling like he had failed everyone he loved.
